title: Roll-weld a pipe joint all round in V-blocks, turning the pipe between passes, after tacking it in locking welding pliers
instruction: Slide the loose pipe along its V-block until its end meets the other pipe's end. The welding pliers are locked on their stand: squeeze their handles hard to unlock them, ease your grip so their jaws spring open, put them over the joint and squeeze the handles shut to lock them on. With the pliers on, tack the joint through the slots in the pliers' bands, at least 1 s of arc on each of at least three 10-degree stretches, turning the pipes in their V-blocks as needed but never tipping the pliers more than about 30 degrees from upright (further, their weight rolls the pipes over). Then set the pliers upright, squeeze the handles hard to unlock them and lock them back on their stand. Weld the rest of the joint all the way round, turning the pipes to bring each part on top. Finish with the gun on its rest and both hands clear.
context: Fabricators join short pipe runs this way: the ends are butted in V-blocks and held in line by pipe-welding locking pliers, the joint is tacked through the windows in the pliers' bands, and once the tacks hold the pliers come off and the joint is welded all round, turning the pipe so each part is welded on top. It takes both hands: one turns and steadies the pipe while the other keeps the gun at the joint, and the top-heavy pliers must be worked so they neither roll the pipe nor block the gun.
setup: Positions in cm: x forward from the arm bases' midpoint, y toward the left arm, heights above the table. Two 1 1/2 in NPS Schedule 40 aluminium pipes (6061-T6; 48.3 mm outside, 3.7 mm wall, 30 cm long, 0.42 kg each), each with one end bevelled 37.5 degrees with a 1.6 mm land and wire-brushed bright 15 mm back from it, lie along y with their axes at x 19, 3.45 cm up, each resting in a steel 90-degree V-block (4 cm long, a relief slot along the V's bottom), the blocks centred at y -26 and +26. The fixed pipe runs from y 0 to +30, bevel facing -y; the loose pipe from y -33 to -3, bevel facing +y (a 3 cm gap). Steel end stops (6 mm plates, 4 x 6 cm) stand just past the pipes' outer ends at y -33.6 and +30.6. The fixed pipe carries painted marks 1, 2 and 3 at 120 degrees beside its outer end (1 on top) and a scribed ring 12 mm from the joint ticked every 30 degrees (12 segments). Welding pliers (JTLD pipe-welding locking pliers for 1 1/2 in pipe, sold on Alibaba; stainless steel, 0.5 kg, 186 mm from band bottom to screw): Vise-Grip-style locking pliers whose jaws end in two half-ring bands (49.9 mm inside, 5 mm thick, 44 mm wide), each band wrapping 5-150 degrees round its side of the pipe; each band is slotted from its tip to 40 degrees from the top (a 20 mm slot), so with the pliers on only the joint's top 80 degrees, under the pliers' head, is covered. The jaw screw is preset for this pipe; squeezing the handles shut to lock them, or pressing the release trigger to unlock them, takes about 20-30 N at the grips (typical for locking pliers this size). The handles have 36 mm wide knurled grips, the movable one faced by a red release-trigger plate. They stand locked, upright, on their stand at x 19, y +42: a 10 cm stub of the same pipe on a steel foot, axis 3.45 cm up. MIG gun (an MB15AK torch, about $130, 0.6 kg, its cable on an overhead balancer): a 15 cm insulated handle (black, 32 mm) and a curved neck to a 16 mm copper nozzle, 1.0 mm wire sticking out 10 mm, lying on a steel rest at x 10, y -30 with the handle along y, nozzle toward +y. The screenshot shows the start. Real trial: the MB15AK gun, fitted with a Teflon liner for the 1.0 mm aluminium wire, plugged into the Euro torch socket of any budget MIG (GMAW) welder rated for aluminium (about $200-400); 1.0 mm ER4043 wire, 100% argon at 15 L/min, settings fixed by a 50 mm test bead on the same pipe; the pipes earthed through the work clamp on a V-block. The supervisor, outside the curtains, holds a hold-to-run switch wired to the gun's trigger socket (the arc can't strike without it), closed whenever the wire tip is within 1 cm of the joint and open otherwise, so it decides only when the arc may strike, never where the gun goes; and an emergency stop that cuts the robots' power and the welder's output. Welding curtains (EN ISO 25980, at least 1.8 m) close the cell with nobody inside while the arc can strike; each arm wears an aluminised glass-fibre cover from base to wrist, each gripper finger a ceramic-fibre sleeve rated to 1200 C for the whole task; a welding blanket covers the table; a fume extractor hood (100 mm or larger) sits within 30 cm of the joint, running throughout; cameras sit behind auto-darkening welding filters (shade 5-8 only while the arc is struck, clear between passes) and cover glass.
scoring: A segment is one of the joint's 12 30-degree stretches between the ring's ticks. Simulation: the held gun's wire tip heats the joint where it is within 4 mm of it, both along the pipe and from its surface, with the pipe ends butted (gap under 2 mm); a segment is welded (turns orange) once the tip has spent at least 1 s over each third of it (10 degrees, 4.2 mm) and 3 s over it in all, and burned through (never counts) after more than 5 s; with the pliers locked on the joint, each 10-degree third that gets its 1 s is a tack, so 3 tacks are at least 3 such thirds, side by side or apart (a bead of at least 12.6 mm, or shorter beads adding up to it). 0 if a pipe leaves its V-block (its axis more than 15 mm from where the block holds it, or its end less than 1 cm onto the block) or the pliers or the gun fall off the table. Otherwise 0.9 x the fraction of the 12 segments welded (rounded to 0.001), capped at 0.5 if there are fewer than 3 tacks or if the pipes are out of line (axes over 0.8 mm or 1 degree apart). 1.0 when all 12 are welded and the pliers are locked back on their stand (centre within 2 cm of where they started), the gun is on its rest (handle centre within 2 cm, turned under 20 degrees), both hands (gripper centre points) are 6 cm or more from the pipes, pliers and gun, and all of them are still, held for 1 s. Real trial: a segment counts when its bead covers the joint over its whole length (both edges at least 1.5 mm past the bevels, no hole through the wall with a lamp in the bore, no crack, no pore over 1 mm), checked with a weld gauge, a 10x loupe and photographs; tacks are counted from the video: the arc on for at least 1 s over each of at least three different 10-degree stretches of the joint (4.2 mm each, located by the ring's ticks) while the pliers are on; in line is checked with a 300 mm straightedge along the pipe at four places 90 degrees apart (no gap over 0.8 mm) after the pipe cools under 50 C.
reset_notes: Simulation: fixed starting poses, no randomisation; the weld and the tack record are cleared at reset. Real trial, consumed each time: two new pipes, bevelled, brushed, marked and ticked as in the setup; re-set the pliers' jaw screw if moved and lock them on the stand; trim the wire to 10 mm and clear the nozzle. Handle the welded pipe only with gloves or tongs until it is under 50 C (about 10 minutes). Brush spatter off the arm and finger covers and the blanket and replace any that are holed.
fidelity: PhysX at 240 Hz. Rigid pipes, pliers and gun with real contact; the V-blocks and end stops are fixed. The pliers' toggle is a spring hinge: squeezed shut it locks (stiff spring); once the trigger has sprung back out, a squeeze that presses it in unlocks it. Locked over the joint, the bands centre the pliers and pull the pipes into line (a constraint). Arc, heat, wire feed, bead shape and distortion aren't simulated: a segment is welded by the time the wire tip spends at it (3 to 5 s; see scoring); 3 tacks join the pipes rigidly. The simulated pliers' fixed band is cut back to 90 degrees (the real one wraps to 150), so they go on and come off straight down, and their release trigger takes about 36 N to press, more than the 20-30 N estimated for the real pliers but within the arms' ~40 N. Not modelled: spatter, cable drag, arm covers; finger sleeves are thicker grippier pads.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0; scripted demo: 1.0 (success at step 6,118)
